claim: Motor neurons are dispensable for proper connectivity in the vestibular reflex circuit that stabilizes gaze.
source: Here, we discovered that motor neurons are dispensable for proper connectivity in the vestibular reflex circuit that stabilizes gaze.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by functional, anatomical, and molecular data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Projection neurons show normal responses and topography after constitutive loss of extraocular motor neuron partners.
source: We first measured activity following vestibular sensation in pre-motor projection neurons after constitutive loss of their extraocular motor neuron partners. We observed normal responses and topography indicative of unchanged functional connectivity between sensory neurons and projection neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing comparable tilt responses and spatial organization in phox2a mutants versus controls.

claim: Projection neurons remain anatomically and molecularly poised to connect appropriately with their downstream partners in the absence of motor neurons.
source: Next, we show that projection neurons remain anatomically and molecularly poised to connect appropriately with their downstream partners.
evidence: Supported by retrograde labeling, axon imaging, and in situ hybridization for pre-synaptic markers.

claim: The transcriptional signatures that typify projection neurons develop independently of motor partners.
source: Lastly, we show that the transcriptional signatures that typify projection neurons develop independently of motor partners.
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA sequencing showing minimal differential gene expression between phox2a mutants and controls.

claim: The current model that connectivity in the circuit for gaze stabilization is retrogradely determined by motor partner-derived signals is overturned.
source: Our findings comprehensively overturn a long-standing model: that connectivity in the circuit for gaze stabilization is retrogradely determined by motor partner-derived signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective experimental findings that contradict the retrograde model.

claim: The vertebrate vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit consists of three neuron types: peripheral sensory, central projection, and extraocular motor neurons.
source: The vertebrate vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit consists of three neuron types – peripheral sensory, central projection, and extraocular motor neurons – that stabilize gaze after head/body tilts (Figure 1A; Szentágothai, 1964).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circuit architecture, supported by citation.

claim: Directionally-tuned sensory neurons innervate nose-up/nose-down subtypes of projection neurons, which in turn innervate specific motor neurons that selectively control either eyes-down or eyes-up muscles.
source: Subtype fate, anatomical connectivity, and function are inextricably linked: directionally-tuned sensory neurons innervate nose-up/nose-down subtypes of projection neurons, which in turn innervate specific motor neurons that selectively control either eyes-down or eyes-up muscles (Straka et al., 2001; Diaz et al., 2003; Glover, 2003; Bianco et al., 2012; Schoppik et al., 2017; Bagnall and Schoppik, 2018; Diaz and Puelles, 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Goldblatt et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the established connectivity pattern of the circuit, supported by multiple citations.

claim: phox2a is a highly-conserved transcription factor that specifies nIII/nIV fate.
source: A single highly-conserved transcription factor, phoxa, specifies nIII/nIV fate (Guo et al., 1999; Coppola et al., 2005; Hasan et al., 2010; Nakano et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit, phox2a is exclusively expressed in nIII/nIV motor neurons but not its upstream partners.
source: In the vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit, phox2a is exclusively expressed in nIII/nIV motor neurons but not its upstream partners (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: phox2a null mutants exhibit exotropic eyes (rotated towards the ears) reflecting a loss of motor neurons in nIII/nIV.
source: Consistent with prior reports and human mutations (Bosley et al., 2006), both eyes in phox2a null mutants were exotropic (rotated towards the ears) reflecting a loss of motor neurons in nIII/nIV.
evidence: This is an observed phenotype consistent with prior literature.

claim: phox2a mutants failed to hatch from their chorions without manual intervention and did not inflate their swim bladders by 5 days post-fertilization.
source: phox2a mutants failed to hatch from their chorions without manual intervention and did not inflate their swim bladders by 5 days post-fertilization (dpf; Figure 1D), phenotypes not previously reported (Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a newly observed phenotype shown in Figure 1D.

claim: phox2a null mutants do not survive past 7 dpf.
source: Consequently, null mutants do not survive past 7 dpf.
evidence: This is an observed outcome of the mutation.

claim: In phox2a mutants, there is a near-total loss of isl1 expression in nIII/nIV at 5 dpf (WT: 298±19 neurons; null: 19±11 neurons; p=2.5 × 10–4).
source: In phox2a mutants, we observed an expected and near-total loss of isl1 expression (WT: 298±19 neurons across both hemispheres; null: 19±11 neurons; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=2.5 × 10–4) at 5 dpf, well-after nIII/nIV differentiation is complete (Greaney et al., 2017).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell counting experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: nIII/nIV neurons in phox2a mutants failed to express vachta at 2 dpf.
source: Unlike sibling controls, nIII/nIV neurons in phox2a mutants failed to express vachta, validating that loss of phox2a perturbs at least two key transcriptional markers of nIII/nIV fate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: phox2a heterozygotes have slightly fewer neurons (229±20 neurons) compared to wildtype (298±19 neurons; p=6.7 × 10–4).
source: Unexpectedly, we also observed slightly fewer neurons in phox2a heterozygotes (heterozygote: 229±20 neurons; Wilcoxon rank sum test against WT, p=6.7 × 10–4).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell counting experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: In phox2a heterozygotes, loss of isl1 fluorescence was restricted to the medial domain of dorsal nIII, which contains some of the earliest-born neurons in nIII/nIV.
source: In heterozygotes, loss of isl1 fluorescence was restricted to the medial domain of dorsal nIII, which contains some of the earliest-born neurons in nIII/nIV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C; Greaney et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C and citation.

claim: phox2a acts in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner to specify nIII motor pool fate.
source: We conclude that phox2a acts in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner to specify nIII motor pool fate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that heterozygotes lose specific early-born neurons.

claim: There was no change in the number of projection neurons observed between phox2a mutants (39 ± 3 neurons per hemisphere) and sibling controls (42 ± 4 neurons per hemisphere; p=0.22).
source: There was no change in the number of projection neurons observed across N=5 sibling controls and phox2a mutants (mean control number: 42 ± 4 neurons per hemisphere; mean in phox2a mutants: 39 ± 3 neurons; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.22).
evidence: This is quantitative data from calcium imaging experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Comparable ratios of projection neuron subtypes were observed between siblings (46% nose-down, 47% nose-up, 7% untuned) and phox2a mutants (49% nose-down, 44% nose-up, 7% untuned).
source: We observed comparable ratios of projection neuron subtypes (sib: 46% nose-down, 47% nose-up, 7% untuned; phox2a: 49% nose-down, 44% nose-up, 7% untuned; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Global spatial separation between projection neuron subtypes remained significant in phox2a mutants (p=0.004).
source: Global spatial separation between subtypes remained significant in phox2a mutants (one-way multivariate ANOVA, p=0.004).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of spatial mapping data.

claim: Nose-down neurons were comparably distributed between null and control larvae (p=0.15).
source: Nose-down neurons were comparably distributed between null and control larvae (one-way multivariate ANOVA, p=0.15).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of spatial mapping data.

claim: A minor lateral shift to nose-up neurons was observed in null mutants (median mediolateral position, sib: 15.2 µm; phox2a: 13.2 µm; p=3.0 × 10–4).
source: We observed a minor lateral shift to nose-up neurons in null mutants (median mediolateral position, sib: 15.2 µm from medial edge; phox2a, 13.2 µm; two-tailed, two-sample KS test, p=3.0 × 10–4) but no changes in other spatial axes (dorsoventral: p=0.16; rostrocaudal: p=0.56).
evidence: This is quantitative spatial mapping data with statistical analysis.

claim: The small medial deviation (2 µm across a 40 µm space) in nose-up neurons is within the limits of registration error.
source: The small medial deviation (2 µm across a 40 µm space) is within the limits of our registration error.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed spatial shift in context of experimental limitations.

claim: Projection neuron topography is established independently of motor partners.
source: We conclude that projection neuron topography is established independently of motor partners.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that topography is largely preserved in phox2a mutants.

claim: Projection neurons responded to tilt sensations with comparable magnitudes between siblings and phox2a mutants (nose-down mean ΔF/F, sib: 1.86±1.69; phox2a: 2.07±1.48; p=0.98; nose-up mean ΔF/F, sib: 1.24±1.23; phox2a: 1.02±0.89; p=0.18).
source: Projection neurons responded to tilt sensations with comparable magnitudes (Figure 2G–J) (nose-down mean ΔF/F, sib: 1.86±1.69; phox2a: 2.07±1.48; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.98; nose-up mean ΔF/F, sib: 1.24±1.23; phox2a: 1.02±0.89; p=0.18).
evidence: This is quantitative calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G–J.

claim: Directional selectivity remained unchanged in phox2a mutants (nose-down mean index, sib: 0.73±0.29; phox2a: 0.68±0.29; p=0.85; nose-up mean index, sib: 0.85±0.26; phox2a: 0.81±0.29; p=0.12).
source: Directional selectivity remained unchanged in phox2a mutants (Figure 2H–K) (nose-down mean index, sib: 0.73±0.29; phox2a: 0.68±0.29; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.85; nose-up mean index, sib: 0.85±0.26; phox2a: 0.81±0.29; p=0.12).
evidence: This is quantitative calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2H–K.

claim: The functional responses of projection neurons and connectivity with utricular afferents are not shaped by motor partners.
source: Collectively, this demonstrates that the functional responses of projection neurons and, by inference, connectivity with utricular afferents are not shaped by motor partners.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that tilt responses are preserved in phox2a mutants.

claim: Projection neurons responded to impulses in comparable ratios between siblings (58% responsive) and phox2a mutants (71% responsive).
source: Projection neurons responded to impulses in comparable ratios (Figure 3E) (sib: 58% responsive; phox2a: 71% responsive).
evidence: This is quantitative data from impulse tilt experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Responsive projection neurons remained localized to the ventral nucleus in phox2a mutants (dorsoventral axis: p=0.99).
source: Responsive projection neurons remained localized to the ventral nucleus (dorsoventral axis: two-tailed, two-sample KS test, p=0.99).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of spatial mapping data for impulse-responsive neurons.

claim: No change in calcium response magnitudes to impulses was observed between siblings (mean ΔF/F: 0.33±0.29) and phox2a mutants (0.36±0.40; p=0.85).
source: We observed no change in calcium response magnitudes (Figure 3F) (mean ΔF/F, sib: 0.33±0.29; phox2a: 0.36±0.40; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.85) or lack of directional selectivity (Figure 3G) (mean index, sib: 0.07±0.41; phox2a: 0.06±0.40; p=0.39).
evidence: This is quantitative calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Fate and connectivity between phasic sensory afferents and projection neurons do not require motor partners.
source: Therefore, fate and connectivity between phasic sensory afferents and projection neurons must not require motor partners.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that impulse responses are preserved in phox2a mutants.

claim: In both phox2a mutants and sibling controls, retrograde photolabeling of projection neuron soma was observed.
source: In both phox2a mutants and sibling controls, we observed retrograde photolabeling of projection neuron soma (Figure 4B), supporting that initial axon outgrowth does not require motor partner-derived signals.
evidence: This is data from retrograde photolabeling experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Initial axon outgrowth does not require motor partner-derived signals.
source: In both phox2a mutants and sibling controls, we observed retrograde photolabeling of projection neuron soma (Figure 4B), supporting that initial axon outgrowth does not require motor partner-derived signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the retrograde labeling data.

claim: In phox2a mutants, projection neuron axons remained dorsoventrally segregated at midbrain targets.
source: In phox2a mutants, axons remained dorsoventrally segregated at midbrain targets (Figure 4C, inset).
evidence: This is anatomical imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Projection neurons did not form collaterals to nIII/nIV in phox2a mutants.
source: Typically, projection neurons robustly collateralize to nIII/nIV targets at the midbrain-hindbrain boundary. We did not observe collaterals to nIII/nIV in phox2a mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is anatomical imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Projection neurons still robustly arborized to more rostral, spinal-projecting targets in the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus in phox2a mutants.
source: However, projection neurons still robustly arborized to more rostral, spinal-projecting targets in the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, suggesting they retain the machinery necessary to collateralize.
evidence: This is anatomical imaging data suggesting retained axon growth capability.

claim: Projection neurons formed occasional, small collaterals in phox2a mutants with few (1–5%) nIII/nIV neurons remaining.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we observed that projection neurons formed occasional, small collaterals in phox2a mutants with few (1–5%) nIII/nIV neurons remaining (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is anatomical imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Projection neurons remain competent to assemble with spatially-appropriate targets.
source: We conclude that projection neurons remain competent to assemble with spatially-appropriate targets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that axons are properly segregated and can form collaterals when targets are present.

claim: In both phox2a mutants and controls, robust transcript expression of synaptophysin a, synaptic vesicle glycoprotein, and synapsin I was observed in projection neuron somata at 5 dpf.
source: In both phox2a mutants and controls, we observed robust transcript expression in projection neuron somata at 5 dpf (Figure 4E), well-after synaptogenesis onset in wildtype larvae (Goldblatt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Motor partner-derived signals are not required for projection neurons to develop the necessary components for synaptogenesis.
source: Motor partner-derived signals are thus not required for projection neurons to develop the necessary components for synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that pre-synaptic markers are expressed in phox2a mutants.

claim: Projection neurons remain anatomically and molecularly poised to assemble with appropriate targets in the absence of motor neurons.
source: Although motor neurons may play later roles in selecting and/or refining pre-motor input specificity, our data supports that projection neurons remain anatomically and molecularly poised to assemble with appropriate targets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective anatomical and molecular data.

claim: Absent collaterals and synapses reflect a lack of adhesive contact necessary to stabilize, but not instruct the formation of nascent structures.
source: We predict that absent collaterals and synapses reflect a lack of adhesive contact necessary to stabilize (Dalva et al., 2007, Moreland and Poulain, 2022), but not instruct the formation of nascent structures.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the anatomical findings, supported by citations.

claim: There were strikingly few differentially-expressed genes in projection neurons between phox2a siblings and null mutants.
source: There were strikingly few differentially-expressed genes in projection neurons between phox2a siblings and null mutants (Figure 5C, Table 3).
evidence: This is data from bulk RNA sequencing shown in Figure 5C and Table 3.

claim: All candidate differentially-expressed genes were lowly-expressed (detected in <10% of reference projection neurons).
source: All candidate differentially-expressed genes were lowly-expressed (detected in <10% of reference projection neurons, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is data from bulk RNA sequencing analyzed against a single-cell reference atlas, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No differences in expression patterns were observed between phox2a mutants and siblings for eight candidate genes evaluated by fluorescent in situ hybridization.
source: Qualitatively, we observed no differences in expression patterns between phox2a mutants and siblings.
evidence: This is data from fluorescent in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: The top 50 highest-expressed genes in phox2a siblings were highly detected in singly-profiled neurons labeled by Tg(–6.7Tru.Hcrtr2:GAL4-VP16);Tg(UAS-E1b:Kaede), including projection neurons (mean detection in projection neurons: 55%±21%).
source: The top 50 highest-expressed genes in phox2a siblings were highly detected in singly-profiled neurons labeled by Tg(–6.7Tru.Hcrtr2:GAL4-VP16);Tg(UAS-E1b:Kaede), including projection neurons (Table 4) (mean detection in projection neurons: 55%±21%, min = 0%, max = 87%).
evidence: This is data from bulk RNA sequencing compared to a single-cell reference atlas.

claim: Any differential gene expression in the data either reflects noise or contamination from other labeled populations, but not projection neurons in the tangential nucleus.
source: Together, we conclude that any differential gene expression in our data either reflects noise or contamination from other labeled populations, but not projection neurons in the tangential nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of bulk and single-cell sequencing data.

claim: The transcriptional profiles of projection neurons develop independently of motor partner-derived signals.
source: Nevertheless, consistent with functional and anatomical characterization, our sequencing data argues that projection neurons acquire the correct transcriptional profiles in the absence of motor partner-derived signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the minimal differential gene expression observed.

claim: The current model for vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit development must be revised: up/down projection neuron subtype fate cannot be retrogradely established by a motor partner-derived signal.
source: The current model of vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit development must therefore be revised: up/down projection neuron subtype fate cannot be retrogradely established by a motor partner-derived signal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective findings that contradict the retrograde model.

claim: The signals that specify projection neuron fate must lie elsewhere, not from motor partners.
source: Instead, the signals that specify fate must lie elsewhere.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that motor neurons are dispensable for fate specification.

claim: phox2a acts in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner to specify extraocular motor pool fate.
source: While the primary focus of our work was circuit assembly, we found that, unexpectedly, phox2a acts in a dose-dependent manner to specify extraocular motor pool fate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that heterozygotes lose specific early-born neurons.

claim: In phox2a heterozygotes, the earliest-born dorsal neurons in nIII are lost but later-born neurons in nIII/nIV are intact.
source: Key evidence comes from phox2a heterozygotes, in which the earliest-born dorsal neurons in nIII are lost but later-born neurons in nIII/nIV are intact.
evidence: This is data from cell counting and spatial mapping experiments.

claim: Partial phox2a dosage preferentially targets the earliest-born neurons.
source: Specifically, if phox2a is expressed in neural progenitor cells that give rise to nIII/nIV, then the earliest-born motor neurons would have the shortest exposure to phox2a.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the dose-dependent effect.

claim: Extraocular motor neuron axons do not serve as 'pioneers' for pre-motor axon targeting.
source: We find that extraocular motor neuron axons do not serve as 'pioneers' (Supèr et al., 1998, McConnell et al., 1989, Bentley and Keshishian, 1982, Bate, 1976, Pike et al., 1992), with pre-motor axon targeting following passively from motor-derived pathfinding signals (Matise and Lance-Jones, 1996).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that projection neurons still establish appropriate projections in the absence of motor neurons.

claim: Projection neurons still establish long-range (hindbrain to midbrain) axonal projections with appropriate spatial segregation in the absence of motor neurons.
source: Instead, we observed that projection neurons still establish long-range (hindbrain to midbrain) axonal projections, with appropriate spatial segregation that matches the topography of their motor partners (Greaney et al., 2017, Liu et al., 2022, Goldblatt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is data from anatomical imaging experiments.

claim: The proper spatial and temporal segregation of projection neuron axons suggests they remain poised to wire with spatially-appropriate targets.
source: Here, the proper spatial and temporal segregation of projection neuron axons suggests they remain poised to wire with spatially-appropriate (dorsal/ventral pools) targets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical imaging data.

claim: Projection neuron axons do not require a target-derived cue to grow, search, and synapse onto motor targets, and simply lack the adhesive contact necessary to stabilize nascent structures.
source: We predict that projection neuron axons do not require a target-derived cue to grow, search, and synapse onto motor targets, and simply lack the adhesive contact necessary to stabilize nascent structures (reviewed in Dalva et al., 2007; Moreland and Poulain, 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the anatomical findings, supported by citations.

claim: Extraocular motor neurons might still play an active or passive role in selecting and/or refining input specificity from their projection neuron partners.
source: Nevertheless, extraocular motor neurons might still play an active or passive role in selecting and/or refining input specificity from their projection neuron partners.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential roles not tested in this study.

claim: Projection neurons also contact neurons in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC/nMLF).
source: We note that our study does not eliminate one additional source of post-synaptic partner signals to projection neurons. As in primates (McCrea et al., 1987), projection neurons also contact neurons in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal, also known as the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (INC/nMLF; Bianco et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circuit connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: Projection neuron connectivity to INC/nMLF targets is present and functional in phox2a mutants.
source: As we did not observe postural deficits in phox2a mutants, we infer that projection neuron connectivity to INC/nMLF targets is present and functional.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of postural deficits.

claim: The development of projection neuron collaterals and synapses to INC/nMLF neurons appeared qualitatively normal in phox2a mutants.
source: Correspondingly, the development of projection neuron collaterals and synapses to INC/nMLF neurons appeared qualitatively normal in phox2a mutants, supporting our interpretation that projection neurons retain the capacity to properly assemble with post-synaptic targets even though similar structures to extraocular motor neurons are absent.
evidence: This is anatomical imaging data.

claim: The tight links between birth order, somatic position, and stimulus selectivity across vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit populations support an 'intrinsic' determination model.
source: The tight links between birth order, somatic position, and stimulus selectivity (Greaney et al., 2017, Goldblatt et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2022, Tanimoto et al., 2022, Zecca et al., 2015, Dyballa et al., 2017) across vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit populations support an 'intrinsic' determination model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from established patterns in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Neurogenesis and initial axon targeting develops contemporaneously for sensory afferents, projection neurons, and extraocular motor neurons.
source: Further, neurogenesis and initial axon targeting develops contemporaneously for sensory afferents (Fritzsch and Nichols, 1993, Altman and Bayer, 1982, Vemaraju et al., 2012, Zecca et al., 2015), projection neurons (McConnell and Sechrist, 1980, Maklad and Fritzsch, 2003, Auclair et al., 1999, Glover, 2003, Goldblatt et al., 2023), and extraocular motor neurons (Greaney et al., 2017, Altman and Bayer, 1981, Glover, 2003, Shaw and Alley, 1981, Puelles and Privat, 1977, Varela-Echavarría et al., 1996), suggesting that neurons are poised to assemble with targets as early as their time of differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: An 'intrinsic specification' model predicts that projection neurons and extraocular motor neurons should be directionally selective as soon as pre-synaptic input is established.
source: Importantly, an 'intrinsic specification' model makes a testable prediction about how and when sensory selectivity should emerge across the circuit: projection neurons and extraocular motor neurons should be directionally selective as soon as pre-synaptic input is established.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the intrinsic model.

claim: Evidence that stimulus selectivity emerges gradually would suggest that sensory afferents and/or projection neurons initially wire indiscriminately and that circuit connectivity is refined in time by extrinsic forces.
source: Conversely, evidence that stimulus selectivity emerges gradually would suggest that sensory afferents and/or projection neurons initially wire indiscriminately and that circuit connectivity is refined in time by extrinsic forces.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

claim: An 'extrinsic' determination model would predict that connectivity is established by an anterogradely-transmitted signal from sensory afferents to ocular muscles.
source: Here, an 'extrinsic' determination model would predict that connectivity is established by an anterogradely-transmitted signal – that is, from sensory afferents to ocular muscles.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.
